rows.stem: If \(\tan 3\theta = \sqrt{3}\), then \(\dfrac{\theta}{2}\) equals :
rows.solution:
\(\tan 3\theta = \sqrt{3} = \tan 60^\circ\), so \(3\theta = 60^\circ\) and \(\theta = 20^\circ\).

Then \(\dfrac{\theta}{2} = 10^\circ\), which is option (D) \(10^\circ\).

rows.subtopic: HCF and LCM by Prime Factorisation
rows.stem: If x is the LCM of 4, 6, 8 and y is the LCM of 3, 5, 7 and p is the LCM of x and y, then which of the following is true ?
rows.solution:
\(x = \text{LCM}(4, 6, 8) = 24 = 2^3 \times 3\) and \(y = \text{LCM}(3, 5, 7) = 105 = 3 \times 5 \times 7\).

\(p = \text{LCM}(24, 105) = 2^3 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7 = 840\).

\(840 = 35 \times 24\), so \(p = 35x\), which is option (A) \(p = 35x\).

rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.subtopic: Consistency from the Ratios of Coefficients
rows.stem: The value of ‘k’ for which the system of linear equations \(6x + y = 3k\) and \(36x + 6y = 3\) have infinitely many solutions is :
rows.solution:
Write the equations as \(6x + y - 3k = 0\) and \(36x + 6y - 3 = 0\). Infinitely many solutions need \(\dfrac{6}{36} = \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{-3k}{-3}\).

So \(k = \dfrac{1}{6}\), which is option (B) \(\dfrac{1}{6}\).

rows.subtopic: Zeroes and Coefficients of a Quadratic Polynomial
rows.stem: If \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are the zeroes of the polynomial \(p(x) = x^2 - ax - b\), then the value of \((\alpha + \beta + \alpha\beta)\) is equal to :
rows.solution:
For \(x^2 - ax - b\): \(\alpha + \beta = a\) and \(\alpha\beta = -b\).

So \(\alpha + \beta + \alpha\beta = a - b\), which is option (C) \(a - b\).

rows.subtopic: Solving a Quadratic Equation by Factorisation
rows.stem: If \(\dfrac{x}{12} - \dfrac{3}{x} = 0\), then the values of x are :
rows.solution: Multiply \(\dfrac{x}{12} - \dfrac{3}{x} = 0\) by \(12x\): \(x^2 - 36 = 0\), so \(x = \pm 6\). This is option (A) \(\pm 6\).

rows.subtopic: Section Formula and Ratio of Division
rows.stem: The line represented by \(\dfrac{x}{4} + \dfrac{y}{6} = 1\), intersects x-axis and y-axis respectively at P and Q. The coordinates of the mid-point of line segment PQ are :
rows.solution:
On the x-axis \(y = 0\), so \(x = 4\): \(P(4, 0)\). On the y-axis \(x = 0\), so \(y = 6\): \(Q(0, 6)\).

The mid-point of PQ is \((2, 3)\), which is option (A) \((2, 3)\).

rows.subtopic: Section Formula and Ratio of Division
rows.stem: Two of the vertices of \(\Delta PQR\) are \(P(-1, 5)\) and \(Q(5, 2)\). The coordinates of a point which divides PQ in the ratio 2 : 1 are :
rows.solution:
The point dividing \(P(-1, 5)\) and \(Q(5, 2)\) in the ratio \(2 : 1\) is

\(\left(\dfrac{2 \times 5 + 1 \times (-1)}{3}, \dfrac{2 \times 2 + 1 \times 5}{3}\right) = (3, 3)\), which is option (C) \((3, 3)\).

rows.subtopic: Number of Tangents from an External Point
rows.stem: If tangents PA and PB drawn from an external point P to the circle with centre O are inclined to each other at an angle of \(80^\circ\) as shown in the given figure, then the measure of \(\angle POA\) is :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - the circle with tangents PA and PB, the 80 degree angle at P and OA, OB, OP joined; the stem states the data. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
OP bisects the angle between the tangents, so \(\angle APO = 40^\circ\). The radius OA is perpendicular to the tangent PA, so \(\angle OAP = 90^\circ\).

In triangle OAP, \(\angle POA = 180^\circ - 90^\circ - 40^\circ = 50^\circ\), which is option (B) \(50^\circ\).

rows.stem: \((\cot\theta + \tan\theta)\) equals :
rows.solution:
\(\cot\theta + \tan\theta = \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta} + \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \dfrac{\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta}{\sin\theta\cos\theta} = \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta\cos\theta} = \operatorname{cosec}\theta\sec\theta\).

This is option (A) \(\operatorname{cosec}\theta \sec\theta\).

rows.stem: If in two triangles \(\Delta DEF\) and \(\Delta PQR\), \(\angle D = \angle Q\) and \(\angle R = \angle E\), then which of the following is *not* true ?
rows.solution:
\(\angle D = \angle Q\) and \(\angle E = \angle R\), so the third angles also match: \(\angle F = \angle P\). The correspondence is \(D \leftrightarrow Q\), \(E \leftrightarrow R\), \(F \leftrightarrow P\), so \(\Delta DEF \sim \Delta QRP\) and

\(\dfrac{DE}{QR} = \dfrac{EF}{RP} = \dfrac{DF}{QP}\).

The first three choices are all forms of this. The fourth pairs DE with PQ, which does not correspond to it, so \(\dfrac{DE}{PQ} = \dfrac{EF}{RP}\) is not true in general. This is option (D) \(\dfrac{DE}{PQ} = \dfrac{EF}{RP}\).

rows.stem: The measurements of \(\Delta LMN\) and \(\Delta ABC\) are shown in the figure given below. The length of side AC is :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - every measurement (LM 45 cm, LN 72 cm, MN 63 cm, angles 130 and 28 degrees; AB 5 cm, angles 22 and 130 degrees) is given only in the drawing. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
In triangle LMN, \(\angle M = 130^\circ\), \(\angle N = 28^\circ\), so \(\angle L = 22^\circ\). In triangle ABC, \(\angle A = 22^\circ\), \(\angle B = 130^\circ\), so \(\angle C = 28^\circ\).

So \(\Delta ABC \sim \Delta LMN\) with \(A \leftrightarrow L\), \(B \leftrightarrow M\), \(C \leftrightarrow N\) (AA criterion).

\(\dfrac{AB}{LM} = \dfrac{AC}{LN}\): \(\dfrac{5}{45} = \dfrac{AC}{72}\), so \(AC = \dfrac{72}{9} = 8\) cm. This is option (C) 8 cm.

rows.subtopic: Surface Area of a Combination of Solids
rows.stem: If the volumes of two cubes are in the ratio 8 : 125, then the ratio of their surface areas is :
rows.solution:
For cubes with edges a and b, \(\dfrac{a^3}{b^3} = \dfrac{8}{125}\), so \(\dfrac{a}{b} = \dfrac{2}{5}\).

The surface areas are \(6a^2\) and \(6b^2\), in the ratio \(\dfrac{a^2}{b^2} = \dfrac{4}{25}\). This is option (B) 4 : 25.

rows.stem: If the area of a sector of circle of radius 36 cm is \(54\pi\,\text{cm}^2\), then the length of the corresponding arc of the sector is :
rows.solution:
The area of a sector is \(\dfrac{1}{2} \times \text{arc length} \times r\).

\(54\pi = \dfrac{1}{2} \times l \times 36\), so \(l = 3\pi\) cm, which is option (D) \(3\pi\) cm.

rows.subtopic: Probability with Cards, Dice and Coins
rows.stem: A die is thrown once. The probability of getting a number which is *not* a factor of 36, is :
rows.solution:
Of 1 to 6, the factors of 36 are 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6. Only 5 is not a factor.

\(P(\text{not a factor of } 36) = \dfrac{1}{6}\), which is option (C) \(\dfrac{1}{6}\).

rows.stem: If the mean of \(2, 9, x + 6, 2x + 3, 5, 10, 5\) is 7, then the value of x is :
rows.solution:
The sum of the seven numbers is \(2 + 9 + (x + 6) + (2x + 3) + 5 + 10 + 5 = 40 + 3x\).

Mean \(= \dfrac{40 + 3x}{7} = 7\), so \(40 + 3x = 49\) and \(x = 3\). This is option (D) 3.

rows.stem: AOBC is a rectangle whose three vertices are \(A(0, 2)\), \(O(0, 0)\) and \(B(4, 0)\). The square of the length of its diagonal is equal to :
rows.solution:
The rectangle has sides \(OA = 2\) and \(OB = 4\), so the fourth vertex is \(C(4, 2)\).

The square of the diagonal is \(AB^2 = 4^2 + 2^2 = 20\), which is option (B) 20.

rows.subtopic: Zeroes and Coefficients of a Quadratic Polynomial
rows.stem: Zeroes of the polynomial \(p(x) = x^2 - 3\sqrt{2}x + 4\) are :
rows.solution:
The zeroes have sum \(3\sqrt{2}\) and product 4. \(2\sqrt{2}\) and \(\sqrt{2}\) fit: \(2\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{2} = 3\sqrt{2}\) and \(2\sqrt{2} \times \sqrt{2} = 4\).

Equivalently, \(x^2 - 3\sqrt{2}x + 4 = (x - 2\sqrt{2})(x - \sqrt{2})\). This is option (B) \(2\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{2}\).

rows.stem: In the given figure, in \(\Delta ABC\), \(AD \perp BC\) and \(\angle BAC = 90^\circ\). If BC = 16 cm and DC = 4 cm, then the value of x is :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - x is defined only in the drawing, as the length AC. Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
In right triangle ABC with the right angle at A and \(AD \perp BC\), triangles ADC and BAC are similar (they share \(\angle C\) and each has a right angle), so \(\dfrac{AC}{BC} = \dfrac{DC}{AC}\), that is \(AC^2 = DC \times BC\).

\(x^2 = 4 \times 16 = 64\), so \(x = 8\) cm. This is option (C) 8 cm.

rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** A ladder leaning against a wall, stands at a horizontal distance of 6 m from the wall. If the height of the wall up to which the ladder reaches is 8 m, then the length of the ladder is 10 m.

**Reason (R) :** The ladder makes an angle of \(60^\circ\) with the ground.
rows.context: Questions number 19 and 20 are Assertion and Reason based questions. Two statements are given, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The ladder, the wall and the ground form a right triangle with legs 6 m and 8 m, so the ladder is \(\sqrt{36 + 64} = 10\) m. The Assertion is true.

The angle the ladder makes with the ground satisfies \(\sin\theta = \dfrac{8}{10} = 0{\cdot}8\), while \(\sin 60^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \approx 0{\cdot}866\). So the angle is not \(60^\circ\) and the Reason is false.

So the Assertion is true while the Reason is false, which is option (C) Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

rows.subtopic: Number of Tangents from an External Point
rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** If two tangents are drawn to a circle from an external point, then they subtend equal angles at the centre of the circle.

**Reason (R) :** A parallelogram circumscribing a circle is a rhombus.
rows.context: Questions number 19 and 20 are Assertion and Reason based questions. Two statements are given, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Two tangents from an external point subtend equal angles at the centre (the two right triangles they form with the centre are congruent), so the Assertion is true.

A parallelogram that circumscribes a circle is a rhombus, so the Reason is true too. But it is a different result, and it does not explain the Assertion.

This is option (B) Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

rows.stem: If \(4k = \tan^2 60^\circ - 2\operatorname{cosec}^2 30^\circ - 2\tan^2 30^\circ\), then find the value of k.
rows.solution:
\(\tan 60^\circ = \sqrt{3}\), \(\operatorname{cosec} 30^\circ = 2\), \(\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\).

\(4k = (\sqrt{3})^2 - 2(2)^2 - 2\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^2 = 3 - 8 - \dfrac{2}{3} = -\dfrac{17}{3}\).

So \(k = -\dfrac{17}{12}\).

rows.stem: The probability of guessing the correct answer of a certain test question is \(\dfrac{x}{12}\). If the probability of not guessing the correct answer is \(\dfrac{5}{6}\), then find the value of x.
rows.solution:
Guessing correctly and not guessing correctly are complementary events, so their probabilities add to 1:

\(\dfrac{x}{12} + \dfrac{5}{6} = 1\), so \(\dfrac{x}{12} = \dfrac{1}{6}\) and \(x = 2\).

rows.subtopic: HCF and LCM by Prime Factorisation
rows.stem: Find the smallest number which is divisible by both 644 and 462.
rows.solution:
The smallest number divisible by both is their LCM.

\(462 = 2 \times 3 \times 7 \times 11\) and \(644 = 2^2 \times 7 \times 23\).

\(\text{LCM}(462, 644) = 2^2 \times 3 \times 7 \times 11 \times 23 = 21252\).

rows.subtopic: HCF and LCM by Prime Factorisation
rows.stem: Two numbers are in the ratio 4 : 5 and their HCF is 11. Find the LCM of these numbers.
rows.solution:
Let the numbers be 4x and 5x. Since 4 and 5 are co-prime, their HCF is x, so \(x = 11\) and the numbers are 44 and 55.

\(\text{LCM}(44, 55) = \dfrac{44 \times 55}{\text{HCF}} = \dfrac{2420}{11} = 220\).

rows.subtopic: Nature of Roots and the Discriminant
rows.stem: Find the value(s) of ‘k’ so that the quadratic equation \(4x^2 + kx + 1 = 0\) has real and equal roots.
rows.solution: For real and equal roots the discriminant is zero: \(k^2 - 4 \times 4 \times 1 = 0\), so \(k^2 = 16\) and \(k = \pm 4\).

rows.subtopic: Zeroes and Coefficients of a Quadratic Polynomial
rows.stem: If ‘\(\alpha\)’ and ‘\(\beta\)’ are the zeroes of the polynomial \(p(y) = y^2 - 5y + 3\), then find the value of \(\alpha^4\beta^3 + \alpha^3\beta^4\).
rows.solution:
For \(y^2 - 5y + 3\): \(\alpha + \beta = 5\) and \(\alpha\beta = 3\).

\(\alpha^4\beta^3 + \alpha^3\beta^4 = (\alpha\beta)^3(\alpha + \beta) = 27 \times 5 = 135\).

rows.subtopic: Section Formula and Ratio of Division
rows.stem: If the mid-point of the line segment joining the points \(A(3, 4)\) and \(B(k, 6)\) is \(P(x, y)\) and \(x + y - 10 = 0\), find the value of k.
rows.solution:
P is the mid-point of \(A(3, 4)\) and \(B(k, 6)\), so \(P = \left(\dfrac{3 + k}{2}, 5\right)\).

Since \(x + y - 10 = 0\): \(\dfrac{3 + k}{2} + 5 - 10 = 0\), so \(3 + k = 10\) and \(k = 7\).

rows.subtopic: Section Formula and Ratio of Division
rows.stem: Find the coordinates of the points which divide the line segment joining \(A(-2, 2)\) and \(B(2, 8)\) into four equal parts.
rows.solution:
Let P, Q, R divide AB into four equal parts, in that order from A.

Q is the mid-point of AB: \(\left(\dfrac{-2 + 2}{2}, \dfrac{2 + 8}{2}\right) = (0, 5)\).

P is the mid-point of AQ: \(\left(\dfrac{-2 + 0}{2}, \dfrac{2 + 5}{2}\right) = \left(-1, \dfrac{7}{2}\right)\).

R is the mid-point of QB: \(\left(\dfrac{0 + 2}{2}, \dfrac{5 + 8}{2}\right) = \left(1, \dfrac{13}{2}\right)\).

The points are \(\left(-1, \dfrac{7}{2}\right)\), \((0, 5)\) and \(\left(1, \dfrac{13}{2}\right)\).

rows.subtopic: Irrational Numbers and Proof by Contradiction
rows.stem: Prove that \(\left(5\sqrt{3} + \dfrac{2}{3}\right)\) is an irrational number given that \(\sqrt{3}\) is an irrational number.
rows.solution:
Suppose, to the contrary, that \(5\sqrt{3} + \dfrac{2}{3}\) is rational, equal to \(\dfrac{a}{b}\) with a and b integers and \(b \neq 0\).

Then \(5\sqrt{3} = \dfrac{a}{b} - \dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{3a - 2b}{3b}\), so \(\sqrt{3} = \dfrac{3a - 2b}{15b}\).

The right side is a ratio of integers with a non-zero denominator, so it is rational. That would make \(\sqrt{3}\) rational, contradicting the given fact that \(\sqrt{3}\) is irrational.

So \(5\sqrt{3} + \dfrac{2}{3}\) is irrational.

rows.stem: Prove that : \(\sqrt{\dfrac{\sec A - 1}{\sec A + 1}} + \sqrt{\dfrac{\sec A + 1}{\sec A - 1}} = 2\operatorname{cosec} A\)
rows.solution:
Add the two roots over the common denominator \(\sqrt{(\sec A + 1)(\sec A - 1)} = \sqrt{\sec^2 A - 1} = \tan A\) (for acute A):

\(\text{LHS} = \dfrac{(\sec A - 1) + (\sec A + 1)}{\tan A} = \dfrac{2\sec A}{\tan A} = \dfrac{2/\cos A}{\sin A/\cos A} = \dfrac{2}{\sin A} = 2\operatorname{cosec} A = \text{RHS}\).

rows.stem: Prove that : \(\left(\dfrac{1}{\cos A} - \cos A\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{\sin A} - \sin A\right) = \dfrac{1}{\tan A + \cot A}\)
rows.solution:
\(\text{LHS} = \left(\dfrac{1 - \cos^2 A}{\cos A}\right)\left(\dfrac{1 - \sin^2 A}{\sin A}\right) = \dfrac{\sin^2 A}{\cos A} \cdot \dfrac{\cos^2 A}{\sin A} = \sin A\cos A\).

\(\text{RHS} = \dfrac{1}{\dfrac{\sin A}{\cos A} + \dfrac{\cos A}{\sin A}} = \dfrac{\sin A\cos A}{\sin^2 A + \cos^2 A} = \sin A\cos A\).

So LHS = RHS.

rows.stem: A chord of a circle of radius 10 cm subtends a right angle at the centre of the circle. Find the area of the corresponding minor segment. [Use \(\pi = 3{\cdot}14\)]
rows.solution:
Let the chord AB subtend \(90^\circ\) at the centre O, with radius 10 cm.

Area of sector OAB \(= \dfrac{90}{360} \times 3{\cdot}14 \times 10 \times 10 = 78{\cdot}5\ \text{cm}^2\).

Area of right triangle OAB \(= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 10 = 50\ \text{cm}^2\).

Area of the minor segment \(= 78{\cdot}5 - 50 = 28{\cdot}5\ \text{cm}^2\).

rows.subtopic: Probability with Cards, Dice and Coins
rows.stem:
Three unbiased coins are tossed simultaneously. Find the probability of getting :

(a) exactly two tails

(b) at least one head

(c) at most two heads
rows.solution:
The 8 equally likely outcomes are HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT.

(a) Exactly two tails: HTT, THT, TTH, so the probability is \(\dfrac{3}{8}\).

(b) At least one head: every outcome except TTT, so \(\dfrac{7}{8}\).

(c) At most two heads: every outcome except HHH, so \(\dfrac{7}{8}\).

rows.stem: In the given figure, PC is a tangent to the circle at C. AOB is the diameter which when extended meets the tangent at P. Find \(\angle CBA\) and \(\angle BCO\), if \(\angle PCA = 110^\circ\).
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the order P, B, O, A on the line and the position of C are fixed only by the drawing. Page idx 14.
rows.solution:
AB is a diameter, so \(\angle ACB = 90^\circ\) (angle in a semicircle).

\(\angle PCA = \angle PCB + \angle BCA\), so \(\angle PCB = 110^\circ - 90^\circ = 20^\circ\).

The radius OC is perpendicular to the tangent PC, so \(\angle PCO = 90^\circ\) and \(\angle BCO = 90^\circ - 20^\circ = 70^\circ\).

\(OB = OC\) (radii), so \(\angle OBC = \angle OCB = 70^\circ\), that is \(\angle CBA = 70^\circ\).

So \(\angle CBA = 70^\circ\) and \(\angle BCO = 70^\circ\).

rows.stem: The perimeter of an isosceles triangle is 32 cm. If each equal side is \(\dfrac{5}{6}^{\text{th}}\) of the base, find the area of the triangle.
rows.solution:
Let each equal side be x cm and the base y cm.

Perimeter: \(2x + y = 32\). Also \(x = \dfrac{5}{6}y\), so \(\dfrac{5}{3}y + y = 32\), giving \(\dfrac{8}{3}y = 32\), \(y = 12\) and \(x = 10\).

The sides are 10 cm, 10 cm and 12 cm. The altitude to the base bisects it, so the height is \(\sqrt{10^2 - 6^2} = 8\) cm, and

Area \(= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 12 \times 8 = 48\ \text{cm}^2\).

(By Heron's formula, with semi-perimeter 16: \(\sqrt{16 \times 6 \times 6 \times 4} = 48\ \text{cm}^2\), the same.)

rows.subtopic: Sum of First n Terms of an AP
rows.stem: The sum of the third term and the seventh term of an AP is 6 and their product is 8. Find the sum of the first sixteen terms of the AP.
rows.solution:
Let the first term be a and the common difference d.

\((a + 2d) + (a + 6d) = 6\), so \(a + 4d = 3\) and \(a = 3 - 4d\).

\((a + 2d)(a + 6d) = 8\): \((3 - 2d)(3 + 2d) = 8\), so \(9 - 4d^2 = 8\) and \(d = \pm\dfrac{1}{2}\).

If \(d = \dfrac{1}{2}\), then \(a = 1\) and \(S_{16} = \dfrac{16}{2}\left(2 \times 1 + 15 \times \dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 8 \times 9{\cdot}5 = 76\).

If \(d = -\dfrac{1}{2}\), then \(a = 5\) and \(S_{16} = \dfrac{16}{2}\left(2 \times 5 - \dfrac{15}{2}\right) = 8 \times 2{\cdot}5 = 20\).

So the sum of the first sixteen terms is 76 or 20.

rows.subtopic: Sum of First n Terms of an AP
rows.stem: The minimum age of children eligible to participate in a painting competition is 8 years. It is observed that the age of the youngest boy was 8 years and the ages of the participants, when seated in order of age, have a common difference of 4 months. If the sum of the ages of all the participants is 168 years, find the age of the eldest participant in the painting competition.
rows.solution:
The ages form an AP starting at 8 years with common difference 4 months \(= \dfrac{1}{3}\) year: \(8, 8\dfrac{1}{3}, 8\dfrac{2}{3}, 9, \ldots\)

Let there be n participants. \(S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}\left[2 \times 8 + (n - 1) \times \dfrac{1}{3}\right] = 168\).

Multiplying by 6: \(n(48 + n - 1) = 1008\), so \(n^2 + 47n - 1008 = 0\), that is \((n + 63)(n - 16) = 0\), and \(n = 16\).

The eldest is the 16th term: \(8 + 15 \times \dfrac{1}{3} = 13\) years.

rows.stem: In the given figure, PA, QB and RC are perpendicular to AC. If PA = x units, QB = y units and RC = z units, prove that \(\dfrac{1}{x} + \dfrac{1}{z} = \dfrac{1}{y}\).
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - that the lines AR and PC cross at Q, with B the foot of Q on AC, is shown only in the drawing (P above A, R above C). Page idx 16.
rows.solution:
PA, QB and RC are all perpendicular to AC, so they are parallel.

In triangles ABQ and ACR, \(\angle A\) is common and \(\angle ABQ = \angle ACR = 90^\circ\), so \(\Delta ABQ \sim \Delta ACR\):

\(\dfrac{AB}{AC} = \dfrac{QB}{RC} = \dfrac{y}{z}\) ... (i)

In triangles CBQ and CAP, \(\angle C\) is common and \(\angle CBQ = \angle CAP = 90^\circ\), so \(\Delta CBQ \sim \Delta CAP\):

\(\dfrac{BC}{AC} = \dfrac{QB}{PA} = \dfrac{y}{x}\) ... (ii)

Adding (i) and (ii): \(\dfrac{AB + BC}{AC} = y\left(\dfrac{1}{z} + \dfrac{1}{x}\right)\). Since \(AB + BC = AC\), the left side is 1, so \(\dfrac{1}{x} + \dfrac{1}{z} = \dfrac{1}{y}\).

rows.stem: Sides AB and BC and median AD of triangle ABC are respectively proportional to sides PQ and QR and median PM of \(\Delta PQR\). Show that \(\Delta ABC \sim \Delta PQR\).
rows.solution:
Given \(\dfrac{AB}{PQ} = \dfrac{BC}{QR} = \dfrac{AD}{PM}\), where D and M are the mid-points of BC and QR.

Since \(BC = 2BD\) and \(QR = 2QM\), \(\dfrac{BC}{QR} = \dfrac{2BD}{2QM} = \dfrac{BD}{QM}\). So \(\dfrac{AB}{PQ} = \dfrac{BD}{QM} = \dfrac{AD}{PM}\).

By the SSS similarity criterion, \(\Delta ABD \sim \Delta PQM\), and so \(\angle B = \angle Q\).

In triangles ABC and PQR, \(\dfrac{AB}{PQ} = \dfrac{BC}{QR}\) and the included angles are equal, \(\angle B = \angle Q\). By the SAS similarity criterion, \(\Delta ABC \sim \Delta PQR\).

rows.subtopic: Volume of a Combination of Solids
rows.stem: A vessel is in the form of an inverted cone. Its height is 8 cm and the radius of its top, which is open, is 5 cm. It is filled with water up to the brim. When lead shots, each of which is a sphere of radius \(0{\cdot}5\) cm, are dropped into the vessel, one-fourth of the water flows out. Find the number of lead shots dropped in the vessel.
rows.solution:
Volume of water in the cone \(= \dfrac{1}{3}\pi \times 5^2 \times 8 = \dfrac{200\pi}{3}\ \text{cm}^3\).

One-fourth flows out: \(\dfrac{1}{4} \times \dfrac{200\pi}{3} = \dfrac{50\pi}{3}\ \text{cm}^3\). This equals the total volume of the lead shots.

Volume of one shot of radius \(0{\cdot}5 = \dfrac{1}{2}\) cm is \(\dfrac{4}{3}\pi\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^3 = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\ \text{cm}^3\).

Number of shots \(= \dfrac{50\pi/3}{\pi/6} = 100\).

rows.stem: Formulate the quadratic equation representing the total area of the lawn and the walkway, taking width of walkway = x m.
rows.context:
A garden designer is planning a rectangular lawn that is to be surrounded by a uniform walkway.

The total area of the lawn and the walkway is 360 square metres. The width of the walkway is same on all sides. The dimensions of the lawn itself are 12 metres by 10 metres.

Based on the information given above, answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - the plan of the 12 m by 10 m lawn with a walkway of width x on every side; the passage states every value. The photograph above it is decorative. Page idx 18.
rows.solution:
The lawn with the walkway is \((12 + 2x)\) m by \((10 + 2x)\) m, so \((12 + 2x)(10 + 2x) = 360\).

Expanding: \(4x^2 + 44x + 120 = 360\), that is \(x^2 + 11x - 60 = 0\).

rows.subtopic: Solving a Quadratic Equation by Factorisation
rows.stem: Solve the quadratic equation to find the width of the walkway ‘x’.
rows.context:
A garden designer is planning a rectangular lawn that is to be surrounded by a uniform walkway.

The total area of the lawn and the walkway is 360 square metres. The width of the walkway is same on all sides. The dimensions of the lawn itself are 12 metres by 10 metres.

Based on the information given above, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
\(x^2 + 11x - 60 = 0\) factorises as \((x + 15)(x - 4) = 0\), so \(x = 4\) (a width cannot be negative).

The walkway is 4 m wide.

rows.stem: If the cost of paving the walkway at the rate of ₹ 50 per square metre is ₹ 12,000, calculate the area of the walkway.
rows.context:
A garden designer is planning a rectangular lawn that is to be surrounded by a uniform walkway.

The total area of the lawn and the walkway is 360 square metres. The width of the walkway is same on all sides. The dimensions of the lawn itself are 12 metres by 10 metres.

Based on the information given above, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
Area of the walkway \(= \dfrac{\text{total cost}}{\text{rate}} = \dfrac{12000}{50} = 240\ \text{m}^2\).

(This agrees with the figure: \(360 - 12 \times 10 = 240\ \text{m}^2\).)

rows.stem: Find the perimeter of the lawn.
rows.context:
A garden designer is planning a rectangular lawn that is to be surrounded by a uniform walkway.

The total area of the lawn and the walkway is 360 square metres. The width of the walkway is same on all sides. The dimensions of the lawn itself are 12 metres by 10 metres.

Based on the information given above, answer the following questions :
rows.solution: Perimeter of the lawn \(= 2(12 + 10) = 44\) m.

rows.stem: Find the distance of the ship from the base of the lighthouse when it is at point Q, where the angle of depression is \(45^\circ\).
rows.context:
A lighthouse stands tall on a cliff by the sea, watching over ships that pass by. One day a ship is seen approaching the shore and from the top of the lighthouse, the angles of depression of the ship are observed to be \(30^\circ\) and \(45^\circ\) as it moves from point P to point Q. The height of the lighthouse is 50 metres.

Based on the information given above, answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - B (top of the lighthouse), A (its foot), P and Q are labelled only in the drawing beside the decorative photograph. Page idx 20.
rows.solution:
Let B be the top of the lighthouse and A its foot, so \(AB = 50\) m. The angle of depression of Q is \(45^\circ\), so \(\angle AQB = 45^\circ\).

In right triangle BAQ, \(\tan 45^\circ = \dfrac{AB}{AQ}\), so \(AQ = 50\) m. The ship is 50 m from the base.

rows.stem: Find the measures of \(\angle PBA\) and \(\angle QBA\).
rows.context:
A lighthouse stands tall on a cliff by the sea, watching over ships that pass by. One day a ship is seen approaching the shore and from the top of the lighthouse, the angles of depression of the ship are observed to be \(30^\circ\) and \(45^\circ\) as it moves from point P to point Q. The height of the lighthouse is 50 metres.

Based on the information given above, answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the points B and A named in this part exist only in the labelled drawing. Page idx 20.
rows.solution:
BX is horizontal and BA vertical, so \(\angle XBA = 90^\circ\).

\(\angle PBA = 90^\circ - 30^\circ = 60^\circ\) and \(\angle QBA = 90^\circ - 45^\circ = 45^\circ\).

rows.stem: Find the distance travelled by the ship between points P and Q.
rows.context:
A lighthouse stands tall on a cliff by the sea, watching over ships that pass by. One day a ship is seen approaching the shore and from the top of the lighthouse, the angles of depression of the ship are observed to be \(30^\circ\) and \(45^\circ\) as it moves from point P to point Q. The height of the lighthouse is 50 metres.

Based on the information given above, answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the labelled drawing of B, A, P and Q. Page idx 20.
rows.solution:
In right triangle BAP, \(\angle APB = 30^\circ\), so \(\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{AB}{AP}\) and \(AP = 50\sqrt{3}\) m.

Distance travelled \(= PQ = AP - AQ = 50\sqrt{3} - 50 = 50(\sqrt{3} - 1)\) m \(\approx 36{\cdot}5\) m (taking \(\sqrt{3} \approx 1{\cdot}73\)).

rows.stem: If the ship continues moving towards the shore and takes 10 minutes to travel from Q to A, calculate the speed of the ship in km/h, from Q to A.
rows.context:
A lighthouse stands tall on a cliff by the sea, watching over ships that pass by. One day a ship is seen approaching the shore and from the top of the lighthouse, the angles of depression of the ship are observed to be \(30^\circ\) and \(45^\circ\) as it moves from point P to point Q. The height of the lighthouse is 50 metres.

Based on the information given above, answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the labelled drawing of B, A, P and Q. Page idx 20.
rows.solution:
From Q to A the ship covers 50 m in 10 minutes.

Speed \(= \dfrac{50\ \text{m}}{10\ \text{min}} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}05\ \text{km}}{1/6\ \text{h}} = 0{\cdot}3\) km/h.
